title: On Honorable Lawful Marriage
attribution_note: St Symeon of Thessalonica (d. 1429). His treatise on the Sacrament of Marriage, from Premudrostʹ nashego spaseniia. Translated here fresh from the Russian for this edition. Source: https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Simeon_Solunskij/premudrost_nashego_spaseniia/6

pairs.en: On honorable lawful marriage
The Bishop

– Now let us speak about marriage, which by God's condescension is performed among people who wish to live in the world, solely for the begetting of children, and is permitted by reason of what followed Adam's disobedience, which was punished with death.

It is performed so that earthly, perishable life may last until life and immortality come through Christ. And so that the conception, the beginning, and the continuance of people's life may not be without blessing, marriage must receive such blessing from the spotless Church, and those entering marriage must strive, as far as they are able, not to defile it — having joined together lawfully and without reproach or blame — so as to keep it, so to speak, spotless and as it were virginal.

sections.heading: The crowns and the laws of marriage

pairs.en: 240. Why crowns are placed during the marriage

Crowns are placed on those entering marriage, as on virginal and pure people, because they join together undefiled, and also as a sign that they preserved their virginity before marriage. And nature itself bears witness that this is beautiful: a bridegroom joining himself to a bride wishes above all that she be a pure virgin and a wife for him alone. In the same way, he must know that he needs to keep himself a pure bridegroom for his bride and be a husband to her, and not to another. If this is so, then marriage is blessed, and the bed — let me speak as Paul — is honorable and undefiled, and upon such a marriage rests perfect blessing, and Christ is present with it.
If a marriage is unlawful and not free from blame, then how will Christ accompany it — the one who is altogether Pure, and Holy, and the spotless Bridegroom of souls?

So let honorable marriage be far from all adultery and violence, let all fornication be removed from it, and with it the impure and defiling kinship of incest and polygamy; let the ordinances of sacred law remain inviolate, so that it be a law of union and not of dissolution. For those who join unlawfully rather depart from God and are separated from Him, and the breaking of marriage brings confusion into the Church.

Let one entering a second marriage fulfil the canon (epitimia), as the fathers commanded, and one entering a third marriage all the more. And let one who enters a third marriage marry only if he has no children and is not yet forty years old. But to one who is forty or older and has children, a third marriage is not permitted, as the sacred legislation declares.
Thus, everything concerning the marriage of such persons must be performed with circumspection and attention on the part of the heads of the Church.
But let us see how marriage is performed in a lawful manner.
If the marrying couple have parents, then these agree among themselves and set out their views on the matter.

Then, when the appointed day arrives and the marriage conditions are to be recorded, a gathering of honorable persons is arranged to witness what is being done and that an agreement about lawful marriage is being made. For this purpose an official too is appointed, who writes the conditions and seals the document with the seals of those contracting (each of them sets a cross), showing that this matter is from God and begins in Christ. The future spouses themselves and their parents sign the marriage contract with a pen, expressing thereby their voluntary consent, and free will, and that it is Christ who joins them in marriage.

Therefore they first worship Him, and only then proceed to set their signatures: this is precisely because Christ unites those marrying, and these contracts are called cross-contracts, and they cannot be broken without certain lawful causes — such as are required for the dissolution of an already completed marriage. Otherwise the dissolution will be unlawful.

When the time for the marriage comes, the bridegroom and bride appear in the church, because the husband receives his wife from God and His Church. The priest, clothed in sacred vestments, first places an iron ring on the holy table as a sign of the wife's tenderness and purity, then the previously consecrated Holy Gifts, because this matter is performed before Christ and because He will be for them communion and unity in sanctification, and in right faith in Him, and in chastity.
241. That an Orthodox person must not be joined in marriage with those of another faith

Since marriage is performed in Christ, an Orthodox person must by no means be joined in marriage with those of another faith. "For what partnership," the apostle says, "has a believer with an unbeliever?" [2 Cor. 6:15]

On some small table the priest sets a cup of wine, called the common cup, because it signifies like-mindedness, communion in life, and chastity. Then, going out to the narthex or the doors of the church — since the blessing is being begun and the matter is still at its threshold — he performs the rite of betrothal. For this purpose the rings are intended, which were previously placed on the table and serve as a symbol of consent and the sealing of the match.
242. On the betrothal

So the priest blesses God and, after the peaceful petitions — that is, the litany, which is proclaimed because peace from God is necessary for those marrying, and also because they join together in peace and for peace and like-mindedness — he places the husband on the right side, because he is the head and chief of the wife, and the wife on the left, as subject and created from his rib and as having come from the husband.

After the litany the priest prays that God, who gathered those far off into union and blessed Isaac and Rebecca, may also bless those now joining with a spiritual blessing. He mentions Isaac and Rebecca, and not some other woman of the ancients, because no other was joined to Isaac and he took her as his wife from his own kindred, lawfully, by agreement, and lived chastely with her alone. And besides, he was Abraham's only lawful son, born according to the promise and blessed by God. Of New Testament persons no one is mentioned at the performance of marriage, because marriage is not the highest state of a Christian, though it is blessed by Christ on account of human weakness and for the continuance of the perishable world's existence. The highest aim of the Gospel is virginity and incorruption, to which it calls those who have the strength for it.

Then, having glorified the merciful God with a loud voice, the priest gives the wife the iron ring, because it is the husband's, and to the husband the gold one, because it is the wife's, and exchanges them up to three times, honoring the Trinity who accomplishes and establishes all things. Then he joins their right hands as a sign that they have been united in Christ and have become one, and that the husband has received the wife from the hand of the Church. The priest, having proclaimed: "Peace to all," thereby expressing union and like-mindedness, and having commanded them to bow their heads, prays that God, who of old betrothed to Himself a pure virgin Church from the nations — that is, that God bless us, the faithful, and this betrothal, and keep those betrothed in peace and like-mindedness.

Then, having loudly glorified the might, the Kingdom, the power, and the single authority of the Trinity as one and all-accomplishing Beginning and Completer, while the appropriate psalm is sung: "Blessed are all who fear the Lord" [Ps. 127] and so on to the end, the priest leads them as children of the Church in the presence of many witnesses, through the middle of the church to the altar, and sets them before the holy doors, as it were before the face of God, because they are joining together in Him in purity.
243. On the performance of the marriage

Standing before the altar, the marrying couple separate their hands, holding them in front, as those standing before God, and show thereby that they are His servants. They hold candles, which signify their chastity and the grace of God abiding in them. In the same way all the clergy hold candles as a sign of Divine illumination and gladness.

sections.heading: The bishop's role and the second prayer

pairs.en: As soon as the petitions for peace have been offered up (for these come first of all and are said in every sacred rite, for peace from above and because it is necessary that in every sacred rite there be prayer for all), the priest pronounces the first prayer of marriage, entreating the Holy God, incorporeal and pure, who created man and from him the wife as a helper for him, to send down His hand from above and join them to one another. And again he joins their hands as a sign of the final union and prays God to join them in like-mindedness, grant them the fruit of the womb, good children, and a blameless life.
After this, in the exclamation he glorifies the God of mercy, and tender compassion, and love for mankind.

Then, taking the crowns from the altar and blessing them, he places one on the husband's head and the other on the wife's head, beseeching the Lord and God of all to crown them with glory and honor, because they are joining together in Him in purity.
244. On the sponsor at the marriage

These crowns are received by the sponsor standing behind them, and so the sponsor of chastity and like-mindedness, who takes the place of a father and guide in like-mindedness and good marriage; therefore he must be from the Orthodox and God-loving. Having again asked for peace, the priest adds the second prayer, just as the hierarch does also at ordinations.
245. That the performance of marriage is properly the bishop's business

For this too is the hierarch's business, and he performs the marriages of kings, magnates, and other persons. However, it is also delegated to priests, because in the sacrament of marriage grace is not transmitted as in the sacrament of priesthood, but it is delegated with the bishop's permission, and moreover for each individual case of marriage, since to perform a marriage is properly the bishop's business, and without his consent a marriage cannot take place. For the father of the Church is only the bishop.

sections.heading: The Lord's Prayer and the common cup

pairs.en: In the second prayer the priest prays that Christ Himself, who came to the wedding in Cana and by His presence showed it honorable, may also now preserve those joining in marriage in peace and like-mindedness. He prays that He make the marriage honorable and keep their bed undefiled, that He grant them to preserve their way of life spotless, so that, reaching a ripe old age, they may fulfil the Divine commandments.

Then the priest proclaims that all things are blessed and sanctified by Christ. Then, turning to the east, he asks that we may be accounted worthy to call upon the Heavenly God the Father without condemnation. And all together they recite the Savior's prayer in thanksgiving for the matter being performed, in signification of our service to Him as faithful servants, and also to obtain Divine blessings and communion with the Spirit — through the holy flesh of the Son of God, who is the Heavenly bread and through whom also those joining in marriage will be alive, if they set themselves to lead a godly and chaste life. For the Lord, as Creator, is Father of all, including those who marry.

After the prayer the priest again makes an exclamation, glorifying the Kingdom of God, and the power, and the glory, and having given peace, commands them to bow their heads before the Creator of creation.

And he pronounces the prayer over the common cup, saying: "O God, who by Your might created all things and established the heavens, and blessed the crown of Your creatures — having made all things, for You are in all and above all — Yourself also bless this common cup of Your servants here with a spiritual blessing, that they may always be blessed," and he makes the sign of the cross with his hand, and proclaims: "For blessed is the name and glorified is the Kingdom of the Holy Trinity," because It blesses and sanctifies all things.
246. That those joining in marriage must be pure, and receive blessing in the holy church, and commune of the Holy Mysteries

After this the priest touches the sacred Chalice of the Previously Consecrated Gifts and proclaims: "The previously consecrated holy things for the holy." And when all sing: "One is holy, one is Lord" — because He is the one sanctification, and peace, and union of His servants who are joining together — he communes the newly married, if they are worthy.

They must be prepared so as worthily to be wedded and honorably to enter into marriage, because the goal of every sacred rite and the seal of every Divine Mystery is sacred communion. And the Church does well in preparing the Divine Gifts for the propitiation and blessing of those joining together, as if He who gives and is — the Abiding, the Existing One — were Himself present at the marriage, and for their peaceful union and like-mindedness. Therefore those entering marriage must be worthy of communion and, as children of God, must be joined in the holy church — the house of God — as it were before the face of God. For in the Gifts He Himself is present, the one being mystically performed; He is offered and acts as mediator between those joining.

Then the priest gives them the Gifts from the common Chalice, while they sing: "I will receive the cup of salvation." This is done for the sake of the All-Holy Gifts and as a sign of the union of those entering marriage in godly thought about God, and also that their godly thought will be born of peace and like-mindedness.

To those unworthy of communion, such as those entering a second marriage and the like, the Divine Gifts are not given, but only the common cup — for partial sanctification, for good communion and union in God's blessing.

Then, when the prolonged supplication (the augmented litany) has been completed, on which both the newly married are commemorated as already forming one whole and the sponsor as a helper in the matter, the priest proclaims: "For merciful," beseeching Divine mercy for them, and on the other hand instructing that everything has been accomplished by God's mercy.

After the priest has given instruction and exhortation and asked for peace, he pronounces the apostolic words: "Brothers, rejoice always in the Lord," and so on, to: "The God of peace will be with you" [Phil. 4:1, 4–9].

sections.heading: The final procession and the releasing of the crowns

pairs.en: Immediately after this, taking them by the hand, he leads them to the altar and, making a circuit, in joy in Christ sings with the chanters the hymn: "Holy martyrs," as at an ordination, and another: "Glory to You, Christ God, boast of the apostles," because those who have lived piously and chastely are companions of Christ and of His saints, and also because one must be joined not only in the flesh but especially in the soul, through our right faith and God-pleasing deeds of piety, so that the marriage too be true, and the marriage undefiled, and the newly married become companions of Christ and of His saints, especially those who despised the flesh even to martyrdom.

Then the priest adds the prayer for the releasing of the crowns, that He who gave the crowns to those joining as a sign of chastity and a reward for their spotlessness and purity before marriage (since they approached marriage spotless) — that He Himself also bless the releasing of the crowns, and keep the marriage and the union indestructible, so that they may always with one accord bless the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. For God the Trinity by His goodness arranges all things for our benefit.

At last, having called upon Christ that for the sake of His Most Pure Mother and His saints He grant mercy and salvation to all, the priest releases the crowns, and the newly married, receiving his blessing, go home with joy.

So, this is what needs to be said about marriage, and there is no need to say more. For although there are some questions concerning marriage, our time does not permit us to speak of them, especially since the fathers have clearly enlightened us about everything.

Only one thing need be known: that those whom God has joined in marriage, He has joined, and that they are cleansed by the invocation of the Pure One. And so let them keep their marriage mutually undefiled, let them abide in peace and piety and in what they have received from God: union in purity, love in chastity, a shared life in like-mindedness and peace — let them keep these mutually as a pledge, so that they be not called to account for chastity and other divine matters. And let them care not only for the flesh but also for their souls, since they too are twofold and consist of body and soul, which is as much above the body as the imperishable is above the perishable. Therefore let them have care for the virtues, and especially for righteousness and truth, for prayers in thanksgiving to God and for attentive communion "in the discipline and instruction of the Lord" [Eph. 6:4], as the divine Paul teaches. From what they receive from God, let them give alms to their poor brothers, so as to obtain mercy themselves and, together with their children, be accounted worthy of the Kingdom of God.
This is all that we could say about honorable and chaste marriage.
